verses.text: Job again took up his parable, and said,
“As God lives, who has taken away my right, the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter
(for the length of my life is still in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils);
surely my lips shall not speak unrighteousness, neither shall my tongue utter deceit.
Far be it from me that I should justify you. Until I die I will not put away my integrity from me.
I hold fast to my righteousness, and will not let it go. My heart shall not reproach me so long as I live.
“Let my enemy be as the wicked. Let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous.
For what is the hope of the godless, when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?
Will God hear his cry when trouble comes on him?
Will he delight himself in the Almighty, and call on God at all times?
I will teach you about the hand of God. That which is with the Almighty will I not conceal.
Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?
“This is the portion of a wicked man with God, the heritage of oppressors, which they receive from the Almighty.
If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword. His offspring shall not be satisfied with bread.
Those who remain of him shall be buried in death. His widows shall make no lamentation.
Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare clothing as the clay;
he may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver.
He builds his house as the moth, as a booth which the watchman makes.
He lies down rich, but he shall not do so again. He opens his eyes, and he is not.
Terrors overtake him like waters. A storm steals him away in the night.
The east wind carries him away, and he departs. It sweeps him out of his place.
For it hurls at him, and does not spare, as he flees away from his hand.
Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place.

footnotes.content: Job gathers his breath one more time. He has listened to his friends' endless counsel, and now he speaks for himself—not in anger, but in the clarity of a man who knows his own heart before God. There is dignity in this moment, a refusal to go silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As God lives"—Job swears by the very One who seems to have turned away. He will not pretend his suffering is small or bearable. But notice: he calls Him God, not enemy. Even in bitterness, he speaks to the Lord, not about Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While his body breaks, Job holds fast to this truth: breath still fills his lungs, God's spirit still moves in his nostrils. He is alive. He has not yet surrendered the most elemental gift. Sometimes we overlook what remains when we mourn what we've lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job draws a line. His mouth will not become an instrument of lies, even under pressure to say what his friends demand. Integrity is what remains when everything else is stripped away—and he will not trade it for easier words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Far be it from me that I should justify you." Job refuses to flatter his friends' theology to find peace. He will die holding his integrity rather than bow to their demand that he confess sin he cannot see. There is steel in humility when it is rooted in truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "My heart shall not reproach me." Job speaks to the conscience—that inner witness before God. His trial is undeserved, his suffering is real, yet his heart remains clean. He will live with a clear conscience even unto death. What a legacy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job turns now to the wicked—those who oppose the innocent without cause. He leaves their judgment to God. He does not curse them with his own power, but speaks the truth: wickedness carries its own sentence written into creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The godless who turn from the Lord—what comfort do they find when their life is cut short? This is not Job's gloating, but his sober observation. He has learned that a heart far from God is already impoverished, long before calamity arrives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When trouble finds the godless, they cry out—but there is no one to hear them because they have not kept company with the Lord in the good times. Prayer that springs only from desperation falls on ears it never cultivated. Relationship precedes rescue.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The godless cannot delight in God. That capacity has atrophied—or perhaps was never kindled. Job is describing not cruelty from above, but the natural consequence of a life spent looking away from the Almighty. We become like what we worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Job assumes the role of teacher. He will speak plainly about God's hand—what he has seen, what he has learned through the furnace. His suffering has not silenced him; it has given him something true to say.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job reminds his friends: you have seen this yourselves. You know the truth of God's ways. Why then do you insist on your shallow explanations? They have become prisoners of their own doctrine, blind to what lies before them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked do receive a portion—not reward, but reckoning. Their inheritance is the harvest they have sown. Job is not denying this; he is affirming it. Wickedness has its own and terrible payday, written in from the beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even a wicked man's children do not escape the consequences. Bread for the table, futures for the young—all are consumed by the judgment that attends evil. This is not Job's wish, but his observation of how the world is ordered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The widows of the wicked make no lamentation—not because no one weeps, but because the man has left behind such a hollow legacy that mourning cannot grow. Death erases what his life failed to build. It is a silent, final accounting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked heap up silver and fine garments. They accumulate with frantic energy, as if acquiring enough will prove them safe. Job sees through this: you cannot purchase immunity with treasure. Wealth without righteousness is only an elaborate tomb.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All that the wicked prepared—the silver, the fine things—passes to the just. The righteous inherit the fruit of wickedness's labor. It is a reversal that echoes through Scripture: the meek shall inherit the earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He builds his house as the moth, as a booth which the watchman makes." Job uses images from daily life—the moth's fragile cocoon, the watchman's temporary shelter. The wicked man's house is not a home; it is scaffolding. When the wind comes, nothing remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He lies down rich, but the night changes everything. He opens his eyes—if he opens them at all—and finds himself erased. It is the final irony: he cannot take his treasure with him, and death takes him before he can use it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Terrors come like flooding water—sudden, overwhelming, irresistible. The wicked cannot outrun them; cannot buy his way past them. In the night, when all his schemes lie sleeping, judgment overtakes him. There is no shelter from God's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The east wind—a biblical image of judgment, swift and relentless. It carries the wicked from his place as if he were chaff. He cannot hold his ground; he cannot resist. What seemed immovable is scattered in an instant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God does not spare him; the wind does not pity his flight. The wicked flees from judgment as if running from an invisible hand—and in truth, it is God's hand from which he cannot escape. There is no mercy for the unrepentant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men clap their hands at him in contempt; they hiss him out of his place. Readers today hear an echo of this—how history and memory mock the wicked, how their name becomes a byword. But Job's own story teaches us another truth: even the righteous who suffer faithfully find their vindication in God's time, not the world's applause.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
